platforms.calibration_tooling: Three named routes, all read this pass: (1) matsim.calibration in matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools - an ASCCalibrator driving an Optuna study, whose update is literally log(z_i) - log(m_i) - (log(z_0) - log(m_0)), i.e. the classic ASC fixed-point loop normalised on a fixed reference mode, with a pluggable learning-rate scheduler and a TerminationCondition dataclass whose check_termination carries "# TODO: not used yet"; (2) Cadyts, a Bayesian count calibration that adjusts NO parameter and instead adds a utility bonus so agents select the plans matching observed counts; (3) opdyts (Flotterod, TR-B 2017), which approximates point equilibria of the mobsim/scoring/replanning loop, with a Berlin mode-constant example. See calibration_methods.

calibration_method.family: coordinate descent over registry-declared sweeps (unchanged, never run to completion) PLUS, NEW AT THIS HEAD AND NEVER RUN, an implemented ASC log-ratio fixed point - src/calibrate/asc_fixed_point.py. Read from the source at HEAD 781cf41, not searched.
calibration_method.what_the_source_says: src/calibrate/calibrate.py:508-533 runs coordinate descent: per round, per free parameter, per grid point across that parameter's registry sweep, a FULL MATSim run -> extract_metrics -> fit -> a weighted scalar objective over declared _fit.json components, keeping a point only if it is feasible against the C4 occupancy and trip-length constraints; the round stops when the improvement falls below delta. The search space is DERIVED FROM THE REGISTRY, not listed in the script: a field is free only if it is source=assumed, carries a scalar sweep and is not held_fixed. The six mode constants are held_fixed under DECISIONS.md 8.5 and are therefore unreachable from the loop by construction - so this project has NO log(target/modelled) ASC loop of any kind. The one constant that is solved, asc_car_passenger, is solved in a separate module (solve_asc_ride.py:101-121) by SECANT INTERPOLATION ON log(ride_per_car) against the observed passenger:driver ratio, and is reported as a CONSTRAINT, not an estimate. The loop refuses to fit more parameters than the objective identifies (four independent numbers) and cannot read a holdout row by construction.
calibration_method.objective_evaluations: coordinate descent: calibrate.py:433 computes the budget as sum(len(grid(p, points_per_param)) for p in free) * max_rounds FULL MATSim runs; at 25% an arm reaching iteration 100 cost 7.66 h wall, so a 3-point 3-parameter 2-round search is ~18 arms and ~140 machine hours. THE LOOP HAS NEVER BEEN RUN TO COMPLETION. The ASC fixed point is far cheaper by design - TWO arms settle the contraction question - and is the only one of the two that has an evaluation count small enough to state in advance. Neither has been executed.
calibration_method.asc_fixed_point_new_this_pass: src/calibrate/asc_fixed_point.py EXISTS and PROPOSES ONLY; it has NEVER BEEN RUN. It applies delta_i = damping * [ ln(target_i/modelled_i) - ln(target_ref/modelled_ref) ] against car as reference - the same object as the Berry (1994) share inversion and the same expression matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools computes verbatim, with the damping declared on CAL.asc.damping. THREE DESIGN CHOICES ARE UNUSUAL AND WORTH RECORDING: (1) THE TEST IS THE CONTRACTION, NOT THE SHARES - two damped rounds are compared mode by mode, and if |delta| shrinks the residual is a taste that constants will close, while if it does not shrink the deficit is STRUCTURAL and no constant will ever close it. That is a cheap, decisive, published-in-spirit answer to the 'constant or mechanism' question that the agency protocol answers only by ordering. (2) It CANNOT REACH A FROZEN CONSTANT: it reads held_fixed from the registry and refuses, structurally, the way the holdout guard refuses. (3) On heavy rail and light rail the step is marked basis_is_boardings and reported as a PROXY, because the logit inversion is exact only for shares of a common total. ROUND 1 IS PROPOSED OFF THE F31 GATE AND NOT APPLIED: bike -0.5121, bus -0.2301, ferry +0.6713, light rail +0.4143.

calibration_methods.implemented_in: matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools, matsim.calibration.ASCCalibrator, driving an Optuna study
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: the alternative-specific constant of each mode, all modes at once, normalised on a fixed reference mode
calibration_methods.update_rule: calc_asc_update returns, verbatim from base.py: math.log(z_i) - math.log(m_i) - (math.log(z_0) - math.log(m_0)) - where z is the observed share, m the simulated share, and subscript 0 the fixed reference mode. A learning rate is applied outside this call.
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: one full MATSim run per outer trial; no count is documented
calibration_methods.convergence_criterion: DECLARED BUT NOT IMPLEMENTED: a TerminationCondition dataclass carries abs_error and rel_error, and check_termination carries the comment "# TODO: not used yet". No default learning-rate scheduler is provided; subclasses must supply one.
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: This is the reference answer to 'how does a twelve-mode model reach equilibrium across simultaneous share targets' in the MATSim world - and the leading implementation of it has no working stopping rule.

calibration_methods.family: Bayesian updating of the plan-choice distribution; NOT parameter search
calibration_methods.implemented_in: MATSim (CadytsModule contrib) and SUMO (SUMO-Cadyts); Flotterod, Bierlaire, Nagel
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: nothing in the utility function. "Cadyts does not adjust any parameters when it calibrates MATSim. Instead, it tries to select and execute the optimal daily plans in each agent's memory" - it adds "an extra positive utility" to the plans whose simulated counts match the observed ones.
calibration_methods.update_rule: "In a Bayesian framework, the simulation system alone provides a complete behavioral prior, which then is updated based on the traffic counts." Agent n draws plan i from a choice distribution P_n(i); the counts reweight that distribution.
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: none as such - the correction runs INSIDE the simulation loop, not as an outer loop of full runs
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: The one architecture in the survey that attains a target WITHOUT an outer loop of full simulation runs. It is a counts method, not a mode-share method, but the mechanism - bias the plan selection, leave the parameters alone - is the structural alternative to everything else in this list.

calibration_methods.family: simulation-based optimisation with search acceleration, exploiting the mobsim/scoring/replanning fixed point
calibration_methods.implemented_in: gunnarfloetteroed/java; a MATSim Berlin example calibrates mode-specific constants to overall mode shares
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: any decision variable of the simulation, mode constants included
calibration_methods.update_rule: "approximately solves general simulation-based optimization problems subject to transport simulation constraints"; the heuristic "approximates point equilibria, i.e. reproducible 'relaxed' states with minimal randomness in simulation setups that comprise the iterative 'mobsim/scoring/replanning' logic of MATSim" (Transportation Research Part B, 2017)
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: unknown - the point of the method is that it does not need a converged run per evaluation, but no count was read this pass
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: It is the only method read that treats the equilibrium itself as the object - it does not wait for a relaxed run before scoring a candidate, which is exactly the cost that makes our own outer loop unaffordable.

calibration_methods.method: boptx / octras - derivative-free optimiser suites for transport simulation
calibration_methods.family: evolutionary (CMA-ES, xNES) and stochastic gradient approximation (FDSA, SPSA), plus opdyts and all of scipy.optimize
calibration_methods.implemented_in: sebhoerl/boptx (successor) and sebhoerl/octras; drive eqasim/MATSim (Berlin, Corsica) and SUMO (Monaco)
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: any declared simulation parameter, mode ASCs included
calibration_methods.update_rule: algorithm-dependent. SPSA's defining property: the gradient approximation "requires only two measurements of the objective function, regardless of the dimension of the optimization problem", with all parameters perturbed simultaneously and pair-wise symmetric.
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: unknown - neither README states a count
calibration_methods.convergence_criterion: algorithm-dependent; not stated in the READMEs
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: This is the closest published architecture to what our own coordinate-descent loop is trying to be, and it says the profession's answer is SPSA or CMA-ES, not axis-by-axis search: SPSA costs TWO runs per gradient step whatever the dimension, where coordinate descent costs (points x parameters) per round.

calibration_methods.method: Parallel Bayesian optimisation with early stopping (BOHB)
calibration_methods.family: Bayesian optimisation over a KDE surrogate, with Hyperband as the cheap evaluator
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: "the 'alternative specific constants' for each mode choice", over eight modes: bike, car, walk, ride hail, drive to transit, walk to transit, ride hail to transit, ride hail pooling
calibration_methods.update_rule: "open source HpBandSter package", a "hierarchy of several 1D Kernel Density Estimators (KDE) with a cheap evaluator (Hyperband, a single multidimensional KDE)"
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: unknown; the reported outcome is "a 25% L1 norm for a large-scale BEAM simulation in fully autonomous manner", on the "'Urbansim-10k' BEAM scenario (with 10,000 population size)"
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: Eight simultaneous mode constants, calibrated with NO human in the loop, on a 10,000-agent scenario - the nearest published analogue to our twelve. The cheap-evaluator idea (score a candidate on a short run, promote only survivors) is directly transferable to a 25% arm that costs 7.66 h to reach iteration 100.

calibration_methods.method: CMA-ES inside the MATSim iteration (planParamCalibration extension)
calibration_methods.family: evolutionary strategy on a maximum-likelihood objective, run as a MATSim module rather than as an outer loop
calibration_methods.implemented_in: an auto-calibration extension for plan parameters in MATSim, Ming Lu & Zhang Xiaoming, MUM 2024
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: the planCalcScore (scoring) parameters - general, leg/mode and activity terms - fitted so that a ground-truth sub-population's surveyed plans are the maximum-utility alternatives
calibration_methods.update_rule: "a logit like maximum log-likelihood is used as goal function"; a designated sub-population (strategyName KeepLastSelected) supplies the ground-truth plans, n alternative plans are generated per person, and CMA-ES estimates the parameters, which are written back into planCalcScore before the next iteration. Configured by <module name="planParamCalibration"> with calibrationEndCriteria designatedIteration or reachConvergence ("updating parameters stops when average estimated difference is smaller than 0.001").
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: ZERO extra full simulation runs - the estimation runs inside the iteration. mleIteration defaults to 1000 CMA-ES evaluations per update, all on the cheap likelihood, not on the mobsim.
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: The one design in this list that calibrates DURING the run rather than around it, and it was tested for scale invariance across population fractions - our exact 25%-sample question. Its own caveats, quoted: "The project is still under development and lots of debugging to do"; "It will definitely slowdown MATSim running time"; "Local minimum might be a very tricky problem for CMA-ES".
calibration_methods.tested_on: a street-interview trip-diary survey, Caton, September-October 2023, plus a Gaode LBS commuting array at 100 m grid accuracy

calibration_methods.method: Bayesian calibration with a Gaussian-process emulator
calibration_methods.implemented_in: "Bayesian Calibration for Activity Based Models" (arXiv 2203.04414), on the Bloomington, Illinois activity-based model
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: the simulator's parameters, calibrated "using traffic flow data"
calibration_methods.update_rule: "We develop an approach that uses a Gaussian Process emulator to calibrate those parameters using traffic flow data", with a deep learning dimensionality-reduction model to cope with the "high-dimensional and non-stationary" character of the simulator
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: unknown - not stated on the abstract page; the point of an emulator is that most evaluations are of the surrogate
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: The dimensionality-reduction step is the part that matters for us: twelve mode targets against a large free-parameter set is exactly the high-dimensional, non-stationary case the paper says a plain emulator cannot handle.

calibration_methods.method: SPSA and W-SPSA for simulation calibration
calibration_methods.implemented_in: the general traffic-simulation calibration literature; W-SPSA in Transportation Research Part C ("W-SPSA in practice: Approximation of weight matrices and calibration of traffic simulation models")
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: "SPSA allows for simultaneous calibration of all supply and demand parameters together"
calibration_methods.update_rule: "a pair of new vectors is generated where each parameter is determined by a perturbation with respect to the original value, with all parameters perturbed simultaneously in a stochastic, pair-wise symmetric fashion"; W-SPSA adds a weight matrix W representing "temporal and spatial network correlations" and "has been proven more efficient than its predecessor SPSA, particularly in situations where the correlation structure of the variables is not homogeneous"
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: two objective measurements per gradient step, independent of the number of parameters
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: The single strongest argument against our coordinate descent: TWO runs per step for twelve modes, versus (grid points x free parameters) per round.

calibration_methods.implemented_in: the agency ActivitySim/CT-RAMP tradition (ARC: constants deferred to a separate Model Calibration report) and, per a search index not verified from a primary source this pass, eqasim Ile-de-France (car ASC set to -0.8 "after several steps of manual calibration")
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: It is still the default in agency practice, which is why the BEAM paper opens by saying "manual calibration methods are time consuming".

calibration_methods.method: Coordinate descent over registry-declared sweeps (THIS PROJECT)
calibration_methods.family: axis-by-axis grid search with a feasibility screen; no optimiser, no gradient
calibration_methods.implemented_in: src/calibrate/calibrate.py at HEAD 6cf0ffd (read from the artefact, not searched)
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: only registry fields that are source=assumed, carry a scalar sweep interval and are NOT held_fixed. The six mode constants (C.asc.bus -1.05, C.asc.light_rail -0.75, C.asc.rail -0.65, C.asc.walk 0.35, C.asc.cycle -1.35, C.asc.car_passenger -0.85) are held_fixed under DECISIONS.md 8.5 and are therefore UNREACHABLE from the loop by construction. There is NO ASC-adjustment loop in this project.
calibration_methods.update_rule: calibrate.py:508-533 - for each round, for each free parameter, for each of n grid points across its sweep, run MATSim -> extract_metrics -> fit, score a weighted scalar objective over declared _fit.json components, keep the point if feasible and better, and stop the round when the improvement falls below delta. A separate one-dimensional solve, solve_asc_ride.py:101-121, brackets asc_car_passenger and interpolates by SECANT ON log(ride_per_car) - "where a logit constant acts linearly" - against the observed passenger:driver ratio; that is a constraint solve reported as a constraint, not an estimate.
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: calibrate.py:433 computes it explicitly: sum(len(grid(p, points_per_param)) for p in free) * max_rounds FULL MATSim runs. At the standing 25% sample an arm reaching iteration 100 cost 7.66 h wall (aborted_20260908T100009_300it_25pct), so even a 3-point, 3-parameter, 2-round search is ~18 runs and ~140 machine hours.
calibration_methods.convergence_criterion: round-over-round objective improvement < delta. The loop also REFUSES to fit more parameters than the objective identifies: "refusing to fit %d parameters to %d independent numbers: that is not a calibration" - the objective carries four independent numbers (five HTS mode shares summing to one).
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: It is the only method in this list whose search space is derived from a value registry rather than listed in the calibration script, and the only one that is structurally unable to read a holdout. It is also the most expensive per unit of information: one full run per grid point per parameter, against SPSA's two per gradient step and Cadyts' zero.

calibration_methods.method: Staged / stepwise calibration, with mode constants as A LAST RESORT (the agency protocol)
calibration_methods.family: sequential protocol, not an optimiser - the published answer to 'constant or mechanism?'
calibration_methods.implemented_in: TF Resource (the Travel Forecasting Resource, the profession's shared reference) and the FHWA Travel Model Validation and Reasonableness Checking Manual, 2nd edition
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: each model component in turn, earliest first: inputs (socioeconomic data, interchange travel times), then trip generation, then distribution, then mode choice - 'As each model is calibrated, the results are passed as input to the subsequent step in the modeling process. In this way, the impacts of error propagation are reduced throughout the modeling process.'
calibration_methods.update_rule: THE RULE THIS PROJECT HAS BEEN LOOKING FOR, and it is published verbatim: 'simple adjustments to modal constants estimated using weighted samples should be considered "a last resort" after all other possible causes for error and calibration adjustments have been considered' (TF Resource, Model Validation and Reasonableness Checking / Mode Choice). The same page states the coupling that makes multi-target mode calibration hard: 'adjustments that increase the transit shares may further decrease the nonmotorized mode shares'. It ALSO states, verbatim, that no numeric acceptance bar exists: 'There are no applicable criteria guidelines for checks of mode choice.'
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: not applicable and not published - the protocol is a human ordering of work, not a search. No count is stated anywhere on either page.
calibration_methods.convergence_criterion: none stated; the manual's language is 'reasonably reproduce observed traffic and transit ridership'. The mode-choice page gives no tolerance at all, while the sibling pages DO give them for other components (trip length within 5%, coincidence ratio 0.7 or higher, intrazonal within 3 percentage points, P/A ratio between 0.9 and 1.1).
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: This is the strongest external corroboration the project has for its own hardest rule. DECISIONS.md 8.5 freezes the mode constants and .claude/CLAUDE.md bans compensating constants; the profession's own reference independently calls constant adjustment 'a last resort', for the same stated reason - constants stand for unmeasured comfort, reliability and safety and therefore mask structural error. It also settles that the project's 10% band is SELF-IMPOSED: the field publishes no mode-choice acceptance criterion to be measured against. And its coupling sentence is the multi-target problem in one line: moving one mode moves the others, because shares sum to one.

calibration_methods.method: History matching with an emulator - implausibility and the NROY region (waves, not a point estimate)
calibration_methods.family: set-valued calibration: it returns the set of parameter values NOT YET RULED OUT rather than one best point, and it is natively multi-target
calibration_methods.implemented_in: the agent-based-model UQ literature; the tutorial read this pass demonstrates it on a wolf-sheep ABM with a Gaussian-process emulator, and the same machinery is standard in climate and epidemiological model calibration
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: nothing directly - each WAVE fits a Gaussian process emulator to a design of simulator runs, computes an implausibility for every candidate parameter set, discards the implausible, and draws the next design only from what survives
calibration_methods.update_rule: implausibility, verbatim: 'I(x) = |z - E(f(x))| / sqrt(Var(e) + Var(d) + Var(f(x)))' - the distance between output and observation normalised by the SUM of observation error, MODEL DISCREPANCY and emulator variance. Model discrepancy is an explicit term: the method assumes from the start that the simulator is wrong somewhere and asks only to be inconsistent within that admission.
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: unknown as a total. The tutorial reports 'Three waves of history matching have been performed' on its example and states no per-wave design size, and it makes NO quantitative comparison against Bayesian calibration or ABC on run count. The evaluation count for history matching on a transport ABM is UNPUBLISHED - no source read this pass applies it to one.
calibration_methods.convergence_criterion: the NROY region stops shrinking between waves, or it empties - and an EMPTY NROY region is itself the finding: no parameter value is consistent with the targets, so the model is structurally wrong. That is a formal, published test of exactly the 'taste or mechanism' question.
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: It is the only architecture read this pass that is BUILT for many simultaneous targets and that can return 'no parameter set satisfies these twelve targets' as a result rather than as a failure. Its implausibility per output is computed INDEPENDENTLY per metric, which is the same shape as the board's twelve per-mode deviations. Cost is the barrier: it needs a design of full runs per wave, and at 25% one arm is 7.66 h wall.

calibration_methods.method: Multi-objective formulations - weighted sum with normalisation (standard), Pareto/NSGA-II with the simulator in the loop (rare), epsilon-constraint (not found in transport calibration)
calibration_methods.family: how many targets become one number, or are refused the chance to
calibration_methods.implemented_in: weighted sum is the field default; NSGA-II has been coupled to MATSim, but for NETWORK DESIGN (searching a Pareto set of network solutions, MATSim evaluating each generation's solutions), not for parameter calibration
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: the objective, not the parameters: 'The objective function in simulation-based calibration is often formulated as a weighted sum of squared deviations between simulated and field-observed traffic measurements - primarily link counts, speeds, and travel times', with the explicit warning that 'Performance indicators of experiments should be scaled before importing them into the optimization formula' because different measures carry different units and scales.
calibration_methods.update_rule: weighted sum: one scalar, one search, weights chosen by the modeller and rarely justified. Pareto: a front rather than a point, so no weight need be chosen - at the cost of many more evaluations. Epsilon-constraint (optimise one objective, bound the rest as inequality constraints) is the textbook way to express 'every mode inside 10%' as a constraint set rather than a sum, and NO source read this pass applies it to transport model calibration.
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: unknown in every variant. No transport-calibration source read this pass publishes an evaluation count for a multi-objective formulation.
calibration_methods.convergence_criterion: weighted sum: the scalar stops improving (this project's coordinate descent is exactly this shape). Pareto: the front stops advancing.
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: This project's fit.py already computes a weighted scalar over declared components, so it sits in the mainstream. The gap the search exposes is that the project's ACTUAL goal - twelve constraints all satisfied at once - is a FEASIBILITY problem, and the two formulations built for it (epsilon-constraint, and history matching's NROY set) are not in use anywhere in transport calibration that this pass could find. A weighted sum can be improved by trading a good mode against a bad one; a constraint set cannot.

calibration_methods.method: THE COUNTER-FINDING - 'The Calibration Illusion in Traffic Microsimulation' (Hickert et al., 2026)
calibration_methods.family: a critique of the whole automatic-calibration literature, and the closest thing found to a published statement of what calibration actually costs
calibration_methods.implemented_in: not a method - an empirical study across five parameter categories (origin-destination, car-following, lane-change, simulation and heterogeneity parameters) on small, medium and large networks
calibration_methods.what_it_adjusts: nothing - it measures what the published methods leave out
calibration_methods.update_rule: its central claim, verbatim: automatic calibration is 'largely an illusion' because 'a significant - and unquantified - amount of bespoke manual work is hidden behind these methods.' Its identifiability finding is the constant-versus-mechanism problem stated formally: 'it may not be clear whether the CFM parameters or the OD parameters need adjustment' when calibrating jointly.
calibration_methods.objective_evaluations: STILL NOT PUBLISHED, and this paper is why: the field's reported figures are the optimiser's evaluations, and the unreported figure is the human work around them. Reported comparisons on the small network: simulation-in-the-loop optimisation reached a velocity MAPE of 5.200 +/- 1.519 against a genetic algorithm's 9.588 +/- 1.866; and changing the simulation timestep by 10% 'could more than double' the mean absolute percent error.
calibration_methods.convergence_criterion: n/a. The paper's warning is that calibrating to AGGREGATE data alone under-constrains the model - 'stop-and-go waves' failed to emerge reliably even in calibrated models.
calibration_methods.why_it_matters_here: It corroborates the previous pass's headline (nobody publishes an evaluation count) and explains it: the count would have to include the manual work, and nobody measures that. It also warns directly against the trade this project keeps being tempted into - fitting aggregate mode shares while the mechanism underneath stays wrong - and it supplies a quantified example of a MODEL setting (the timestep, not a behavioural parameter) dominating the result, which is the same class of error as a teleported access leg or an absent crowding term.
